titulo.texto: The Art of Turquoise Mosaic and the Skull from Tomb 7

frase_gancho.texto: A real skull covered in turquoise: the eternal face of an ancestor.

puente_narrativo.texto: From blue stone we move on to transparent stone. Look for a tiny rock crystal cup, so thin it seems like glass, made without a single metal tool.

guion_corto.texto: Mixtec mosaic art reached its peak by covering with turquoise, red Spondylus shell and gold both ceremonial shields, like the famous Chimalli displayed in this museum, and the sacred relics of Tomb 7 at Monte Albán, whose most awe-inspiring piece is the Skull with turquoise mosaic kept in Oaxaca. On it, the royal skull of a high-ranking lord was covered with hundreds of blue and green turquoise tesserae glued on with copal, white shell eyes with obsidian pupils, and a red flint knife in the nasal cavity. For the Mixtec, preserving an ancestor this way was transforming him into an eternal oracle.

guion_largo.texto:
Many people are deeply moved by this piece, and that is natural: here, what is ancient is not just the object, it is the person. This was a real human being, a Mixtec lord, and someone, between five hundred and eight hundred years ago, spent weeks gluing tiny pieces of turquoise onto his skull, one by one. Although the original skull remains in the Santo Domingo Museum in Oaxaca along with the rest of Tomb 7, its image and the turquoise mosaics in this hall reveal how the ancient Mixtec saw death: as an act of reverence toward the lineage.

Each piece was cut, polished and fitted to the curve of the bone, on the forehead, the cheekbones and the jaw. They were glued on with a resin, as in other mosaics of the period. The bands of red shell, which comes from the sea, break up the blue and give it rhythm. Everything is designed so that the skull stops looking like a remain and looks like a mask.

Turquoise deserves a pause. It does not occur naturally in Oaxaca. It was a mineral that arrived from far away, from the north, from regions that today are the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, along very long trade routes. Further on, in the North Hall, you will see one of the cities it passed through, Paquimé. In Mesoamerica, turquoise was the color of the sky and of sacred fire: you have already seen how Xiuhtecuhtli, the Lord of Fire, was also the “Lord of Turquoise,” and how a turquoise mirror protected the backs of the warriors of Tula.

The eyes are made of white shell with a black obsidian pupil, and in the nose there is a flint knife, the same symbol of death and sacrifice that you saw on the tongue of the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol). This is no aesthetic coincidence: these are signs with meaning. The flint knife, in the nose, turns the face into a reminder of what awaited everyone.

Why do this to an ancestor? For the Mixtec, the relationship with the dead was also political. A lord legitimized his power by showing whom he descended from. The Mixtec codices tell the lives of kings and queens as if they were novels of weddings, alliances and wars; one of the most famous, 8 Deer “Jaguar Claw,” lived in the eleventh century. To have the skull of an ancestor close at hand, turned into an oracle, was to have an ally.

The Mexica did something similar. In the British Museum, in London, there is a famous human skull covered with a turquoise mosaic, attributed to the figure of Tezcatlipoca, the god of the smoking mirror. If you compare it with this one, you will see that they belong to the same tradition: covering the bone with the most precious things in the world.

And perhaps it is no coincidence that today, in Mexico, the skull is not only frightening: it adorns, it smiles, it is made of sugar and eaten. Some see in this a very distant echo of this way of looking at death, without hiding it. On the altar for the dead, next to the marigolds, the sugar skulls bear proper names, just as this skull once bore, in its time, a face.

texto: Observe, in the mosaic pieces in the hall and in the image on your screen, the millimeter-precise cut of the blue and green turquoise tesserae
Notice the contrast with the red Spondylus shell brought from the Pacific Ocean
Note how the flint knife and the shell eyes gave ritual life to the face

texto.Material: Mosaic of turquoise, Spondylus shell, mother-of-pearl and obsidian, adhered with copal resin
texto.Origin: Tomb 7 at Monte Albán and the Upper Mixtec region, Oaxaca (discovered by Alfonso Caso in January 1932; the original skull is in the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca)

texto.pregunta: Myth: Skulls with mosaic were war trophies.
texto.respuesta: Reality: This is the skull of a venerated ancestor, not of an enemy: he was honored as the protector and oracle of the lineage.
